doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Studio professionalism and double-booking
summary: Being early and prepared, enjoying the camaraderie versus lonely composing, and covering overlapping dates with subs.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: And it goes without saying that those studio years, you just have to take care of business. You have to be on time, you can’t have attitude, I mean the whole thing.

The whole thing. Yeah. You have to be on time which means you’ve got to be fairly early. Now if you want to warm up properly if you didn’t get a chance to at home. And then you could look at the music ahead of time, and meet the guys. My favorite thing to do is still playing, even though I like to orchestrate. Because orchestrating and composing is a very lonely life. You sit at home, or if you have an office and there’s no one, it’s eerily quiet and I don’t like that. I like a little chatter. But when you’re a musician showing up, “hey, Joe, how’s it going?” Yeah you meet the guys, you tell a few jokes, you know it’s kind of like what you’ve done growing up, sitting and playing in bands. And there’s a lot more camaraderie going on because, like I said, the other part of it — composing — is very lonely. But it’s very satisfying also. So I like both parts. But my favorite thing is just showing up playing and sort of going home. There’s a lot less responsibility. When you are a composer there’s a lot more responsibility going on. And
I’m a responsible person, so that part doesn’t bother me. But you have to plan. You have to plan.
Did you, in the heyday, did you see some student musicians trying to, you know, make two dates at basically the same time — play the system?

Oh yeah. Absolutely. Yeah. And I myself did that in case one gets canceled or then one gets pushed back two, three, four hours, and you could always cover yourself because there’s always somebody good that could substitute for you for something. You call the contractor up and say I’m so-and-so, I’m sorry I can’t — something happened I can’t make this particular session but I have a great sub coming in. You try not to do that, because you don’t want the contractor getting upset ‘cause he wanted you. So the big guys could do that. You know when I talk the big guys — when I first got to town the big guys, you know —
